description:
A spring outside Makkah still carries her name, more than a thousand years later.

In the 8th century, water in Makkah was so scarce that a single water-skin could sell for a dinar. Zubaidah bint Ja’far, wife of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, had the money to pay for water one Hajj at a time. She chose to bring it from a spring at Wadi Nu’man, through mountains and solid rock, all the way to the city.

She was warned about the cost. As the story goes, her answer was: “Do it, even if every swing of the pickaxe costs a dinar.”

The water kept flowing to pilgrims for centuries. People still call it Ayn Zubaidah.

She built a waqf. Give once, and it keeps giving.

"Those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying, 'Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.'" (Qur'an 3:191)

description:
In this episode, we explore one of the most remarkable moments in the life of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — the Expedition of Tabūk, known as Ghazwat al-‘Usrah (The Expedition of Difficulty).

The ninth year after Hijrah brought a test unlike any before. The heat was intense, the journey long, and provisions were scarce. Yet the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the believers to prepare for an expedition against the mighty Byzantine Empire. It was not merely a march of soldiers — it was a test of sincerity, sacrifice, and true faith.

This episode highlights powerful moments from this historic expedition, including:

• The Prophet ﷺ announcing the difficult journey to Tabūk
• The excuses and plots of the hypocrites exposed by revelation
• The incredible generosity of the companions, including the donation of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (RA)
• The companions who wept because they could not afford to join the army
• The touching story of Abū Khaythamah leaving comfort behind to catch up with the Prophet ﷺ
• Lessons from the ruins of Thamūd along the journey
• The peaceful treaties established at Tabūk
• The exposure and destruction of Masjid al-Dirār, built to divide the believers

Although no battle took place, Tabūk became one of the greatest tests of faith in the Seerah. It revealed the sincerity of the believers and exposed the hypocrisy of those whose faith was only on the tongue.

A powerful reminder that sometimes the greatest victories are not fought with swords, but with patience, sacrifice, and unwavering trust in Allah.

description:
In Episode 27 of Life of the Final Messenger ﷺ, we explore the events of the Battle of Hunayn, which took place shortly after the Conquest of Makkah.

After the Muslims entered Makkah peacefully, some surrounding tribes, including Hawazin and Thaqif, feared the growing strength of the Muslim community. They gathered a large force and prepared to confront the Muslims.

The Prophet ﷺ marched with a large army toward the valley of Hunayn. However, as the Muslims entered the narrow valley, they were suddenly ambushed by enemy forces hiding in the surrounding hills.

For a brief moment, confusion spread among some of the ranks. Yet the Prophet ﷺ remained firm and called the believers back to the battlefield. One by one, the companions regrouped around him and the tide of the battle began to turn.

The Muslims ultimately achieved victory, demonstrating that success comes not from numbers but from faith, unity, and reliance upon Allah.

description:
In Episode 26 of Life of the Final Messenger ﷺ, we witness one of the most powerful and transformative moments in Islamic history: The Conquest of Makkah.

After the Quraysh violated the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ prepared a large army and marched toward Makkah. The Muslims advanced with discipline and humility, determined to restore peace and justice.

Along the way, Abu Sufyan encountered the Muslim army and came to realize the strength and resolve of the believers.

When the Muslims entered Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ ensured that the city was taken peacefully with minimal conflict. The idols surrounding the Kaʿbah were removed, restoring the sacred sanctuary to the worship of Allah alone.

In a moment that stunned many of his former enemies, the Prophet ﷺ declared a day of mercy, granting forgiveness and amnesty to the people of Makkah.

This episode highlights mercy, leadership, and the fulfillment of a mission that began years earlier.

description:
In Episode 25 of Life of the Final Messenger ﷺ, we explore the historic Battle of Muʾtah, one of the most remarkable battles in early Islamic history.

The Prophet ﷺ sent an army of 3,000 companions toward the north after a Muslim envoy was killed. Three commanders were appointed in advance: Zayd ibn Harithah (RA), Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib (RA), and Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA).

When the Muslim army reached Muʾtah, they faced an enormous force from the Byzantine Roman army and their allies. Despite the overwhelming odds, the companions showed extraordinary courage.

One after another, the appointed commanders were martyred while holding the banner of Islam. Finally, Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) took command and used his military skill to safely withdraw the Muslim army.
This episode highlights the bravery of the companions, the sacrifice of the martyrs, and the leadership that preserved the Muslim army.

description:
In Episode 9 of Life of the Final Messenger ﷺ, persecution in Makkah reaches a level where faith must seek refuge beyond its homeland.

Abyssinia becomes Islam’s first sanctuary — proof that faith, when persecuted, will always find a place of protection.

Before Prophethood, Makkah trusted him. Soon, the world would follow him ﷺ.

Through every stage, Allah was nurturing the Orphan of Makkah ﷺ — preparing him for a mission that would transform humanity.

Today marks a defining moment in our mission to democratise real estate investing: we're launching Wahed Private Real Estate in the United States! 📣


Real estate represents the world's largest reservoir of wealth, worth $379.7 trillion, yet our community has remained largely excluded from meaningful participation. Structural barriers such as the prevalence of debt and interest has made investing in property generally inaccessible to most Muslims. 


We launched in the UK first, introducing a model for fractional, fully managed, Shariah-compliant real estate investing. Properties funded within hours. Investors began building their portfolios with low minimums. In just a few months, we deployed millions of pounds across properties in the UK.


The US expansion was always part of the vision. Although house prices in the US have surged 54% in the past decade, over 33% of Muslim Americans earn less than $30,000 annually. With rising property prices, but low income and limited Halal financing options, the gap continues to widen for the Muslim diaspora – and so does the need for accessible, Islamically aligned alternatives.


We're addressing a systemic issue that has prevented hundreds of thousands of American Muslims from participating in real estate. With Wahed private real estate, investors can now access fully Shariah-compliant, professionally managed opportunities with as low as $100. 


From London to New York, we're building financial infrastructure for a community that deserves fair and equal access to wealth-building opportunities through real estate.


Join our waitlist: https://tally.so/r/w8VzeP

In Episode 2 of The Believer’s Response, Sheikh Ahmed Umar joins Brother Shahid Hassan to discuss the money decisions facing Muslim households: buying a home, paying for university and finding better ways to earn without relying on Riba.

The discussion also asks why financial relief may be delayed despite your du’a, and how to start putting things right if your finances already involve riba.

How does someone who once seemed so firm lose his way?

In Episode 5 of the Tadabbur series, Sheikh Mohamed Eid Almuhairi continues through Surah Yunus, where the verses move from people who notice Allah’s signs in the smallest things to people who remain heedless even when the signs are all around them.

Then the questions become harder. Can your own actions put your guidance at risk? Why do you ask Allah for the straight path every day when you are already Muslim? And what does it say about a person who begs Allah through a hardship, only to forget Him as soon as it ends?

Surah Yunus asks you to look at what happened to those before you. Then it asks what you are doing with the guidance you have now.

You can know what is right, see the proof clearly, and still choose not to follow it. Abu Talib heard the call to Islam directly from the Prophet ﷺ. He understood the message and knew the language, yet died without accepting Islam.

His story reveals a distinction we cannot afford to overlook: being shown the right path is not the same as being granted the success to follow it.

Allah is Al-Hadi, The Guide. His guidance reaches every living creature. He shows people the truth through revelation and His messengers. But it is Allah alone who grants the Tawfeeq to accept that truth, act upon it, and remain steadfast.

In Episode 12 of Allah's Names and Attributes, Sheikh Muhammad Tim Humble explains the different forms of Allah's guidance, the consequences of turning away from the truth, and why even practising Muslims must continue asking Allah to guide them.

What are we really asking for every time we recite, "Guide us to the straight path"?

description:
Ten years can pass while you are still telling yourself: “One day, I’ll properly seek knowledge.” You blame the lack of time. Your job. Your family. Where you live. The fact that you cannot travel. Maybe even your weak memorisation.

But then you meet or hear about students with those same responsibilities who somehow learnt Arabic, progressed through the Islamic sciences, and reached the point of teaching others!

So what are they doing differently?

In this Majalis Ilmiyyah episode, Sheikh Muhammad Tim Humble and Sheikh Abdullahi Abdisalam speak directly to students seeking knowledge in the West and other non-Muslim countries, and confront some of the habits and misunderstandings that can quietly leave a student stuck for years.

Why can thirty focused minutes sometimes take you further than hours of scattered study? Why do some students keep jumping from one programme to another without progressing? And what should you do when memorisation becomes so difficult that it starts blocking you from moving forward?

The path may be far more open than you think. But are you approaching it the right way?

description:
There was a time when seeking Islamic knowledge meant leaving home without knowing when you would return. The Salaf crossed cities, countries and deserts. They endured hunger, thirst, loneliness and months on the road - sometimes to hear a single Hadith, and sometimes simply to verify one they had already received.

Our brand-new series, Travelling in Pursuit of Knowledge, follows those journeys.

With Sheikh Muhammad Huzaifah, we will accompany the Salaf through the paths they travelled, the scholars they sought, the hardships they endured and the moments that reveal just how highly they valued knowledge and the Sunnah.

These are not stories to admire and move past. They are stories of patience, worship, manners and aspirations that force us to reconsider our own relationship with knowledge.

But before we follow them on the road, we need to understand the road itself.

Why did travelling become such a defining feature of seeking Islamic knowledge?

And what could make a man travel for weeks… for just one Hadith?

description:
We all claim to love our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. But how many of us can confidently say that we have read even one complete book about his life? We know his name. We send Salah and Salam upon him. We speak about following his Sunnah. Yet many of us know surprisingly little about how he ﷺ actually lived - as a husband, a father, a leader and a teacher, through hardship, opposition, loss and victory.

And because of that, many of us have never realised just how much studying his ﷺ life can change the way we think, the choices we make, and the way we deal with the situations we face every day.

But even when we begin reading the Seerah, another question arises:

Are we reading it the way it was meant to be read?

Why was his ﷺ life preserved in such extraordinary detail? And how can events from over 1,400 years ago help us navigate family, work, trials and the struggles Muslims face today?

In this episode of Majalis Ilmiyyah, Sheikh Dr. Ibrahim bin Khaleel Bani Salamah joins Sheikh Muhammad Tim Humble for a discussion on how to study the Seerah, understand it and, most importantly, live by it.

Perhaps it is time we truly got to know the Messenger ﷺ whose love we so readily claim.

But have you ever stopped to ask why Allah places these particular verses together?

The Surah begins with the one who denies the Day of Recompense: someone harsh towards the orphan and unconcerned about the poor.

In this episode of Tadabbur of the Qur’an, Sheikh Mohamed Eid Almuhairi reflects on Surah Al-Ma‘un, drawing out its deeper connections and showing how the Tafseer of the Salaf helps reveal a much fuller picture.

You know the Surah.

Now look again.

It may be speaking much closer to home than you thought.

description:
What if the very thing you are doing to get closer to Allah… is something He never asked you to do? The intention may be sincere. The act itself may even be something beloved in Islam. Dhikr. Salah. Reciting Qur’an. Sending Salawat upon the Prophet ﷺ.

So where could the problem possibly be?

This is where the question of Bid‘ah becomes far more subtle than many imagine.

Can a legislated act of worship become an innovation simply because its time, place, number or manner was changed? If nobody can point to something explicitly forbidden about a practice, does that make it acceptable? And when someone says, “But my intention is good”, is that enough?

There is a striking incident in this lecture where people were engaged in Dhikr and defended themselves with precisely that argument: they only wanted good. Ibn Mas‘ud رضي الله عنه responded with words every sincere Muslim should stop and think about.

Sheikh Dr. Ibrahim ibn Khaleel Bani Salamah unpacks what it really means to follow the Sunnah, how Bid‘ah quietly enters worship, why sincerity alone cannot settle the matter, and the common arguments used to justify religious innovations.

Because sometimes the real question isn’t:

“Is this a good deed?”

It is:

“Did Allah ask to be worshipped this way?”

description:
Why does Allah allow the believers to be persecuted while their oppressors seem to grow stronger? Surah Al-Burooj gives an answer that is far more unsettling - and far more hopeful - than simply saying, “Be patient.” The believers of the trench were tortured for one reason: they believed in Allah. Their enemies watched them burn. Yet right in the middle of this horrifying account, Allah describes Himself as Al-‘Azeez, Al-Hameed - the Almighty, the One worthy of all praise.

Why would Allah mention His absolute power at the very moment the believers appear powerless?

And what if the people we think are “winning” have misunderstood victory completely?

In this Tafseer Juz Amma episode, Sheikh Muhammad Tim Humble unpacks the story of the people of the trench, why Allah sometimes allows oppressors to have power, what their apparent success really means, and why Muslim suffering should force us to look at something much closer to home.

But Surah Al-Burooj does not only speak about what happens to the oppressed. It also reveals what the Ummah must do when surrounded by weakness, persecution and defeat.

description:
What does Iman look like when life begins to hurt? When sickness enters your life, it can bring more than physical pain. It can leave you afraid, confused and searching for answers. Why has Allah allowed this to happen? Is it a punishment, a test, or a sign of His love? And how should a believer respond when patience feels difficult?

AMAU presents The Believer’s Response, a new podcast series exploring how a Muslim faces the moments that shake the heart: sickness, financial loss, grief, betrayal, marital struggles, failure and uncertainty.

When every door seems closed, and the heart feels overwhelmed, Islam does not leave the believer without direction.

In the first episode, Sheikh Abdullahi Abdissalam joins us for a deeply personal conversation about sickness. He explores the wisdom behind illness, what it means to pass the test, how to distinguish natural sadness from blameworthy complaint, and how hardship can become a means of forgiveness, growth and closeness to Allah.

He also shares his own journey through chronic illness - and why, years later, he considers it one of the greatest gifts Allah gave him.

For anyone facing sickness, caring for someone who is ill, or struggling to understand a painful decree, this episode offers perspective, reassurance and hope.

description:
We all say we want to study Islam. To become people of knowledge. But what happens when seeking knowledge begins to cost us comfort? A young Sahabi was told that nobody would ever need him. Years later, senior figures from the Sahabah would sit beside him and listen. Another possessed so little food that he would collapse from hunger; yet went on to preserve more Hadith than any other narrator.

What changed their lives?

It was not talent alone. It was not inspiration. In fact, the Prophet ﷺ had made Du‘a for their knowledge. But there was something else.

In this second episode of Stories from the Golden Generations of Islam, Ustadh Muhammad Tim Humble uncovers the hidden struggle behind the knowledge of ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas and Abu Hurayrah رضي الله عنهما.

Why did Ibn ‘Abbas lie outside people’s doors until dust covered his face? How did Abu Hurairah remember thousands of Hadith after spending only a few years with the Prophet ﷺ? And what does their sacrifice expose about our ambitions?

You may say you want knowledge. But do your actions prove it?

Watch until the end, and ask yourself: How badly do I really want it?

description:
The problem isn't that Muslims today don't refer back to the Qur'an and Sunnah. The problem is that they misinterpret them. Every sect. Every group. Every speaker claims to follow the Qur'an and Sunnah. Each one opposes the others. Yet they can't all be right. So where does the difference begin? Is it intelligence? Is there a principle that many Muslims have forgotten? More importantly, how can the Ummah return to the correct understanding of the Qur'an and the Sunnah?

In this episode of Majalis 'Ilmiyyah, Sheikh Dr. Asim al-Qaryooti, Sheikh Dr. Ibrahim ibn Khaleel Bani Salamah, and Sheikh Muhammad Tim Humble address the question behind countless disagreements taking place in the Ummah: Who has the right to explain the Qur'an and Sunnah, and according to whose understanding?

- Can someone sincerely follow the Qur'an and Sunnah... and still be mistaken?

And what principles protect a Muslim from being misled by those who outwardly say, "Allah said," and, "His Messenger ﷺ said."

description:
Control is something we rarely question. We want control over our circumstances, our future, the people around us, and the outcomes we hope for. It's easy to think that if we could just hold on a little tighter, we'd finally feel at peace. But what if that way of thinking is exactly what's keeping us restless?

In this episode of Fiqh al-Asma al-Husna series, Sheikh Muhammad Tim Humble explores two of Allah's Beautiful Names - Al-Malik and Al-Maleek - and what they reveal about ownership, authority, and the reality of who is truly in control. Along the way, he reflects on one of the Qur'an's most striking questions, a verse that strips away every illusion we cling to and reminds us that every soul, every possession, and every decree belongs to Allah alone.

Whether you've struggled to accept Allah's decree, found yourself asking "Why did this happen to me?", or simply want to deepen your understanding of your Lord, this episode offers a perspective that's both humbling and deeply comforting.

Sometimes, peace doesn't come from gaining more control.

It comes from recognising that it was never ours to begin with.

description:
You memorised it once. So why can't you remember it now? Every hafidh who forgets. Every student of knowledge who studied for years and can barely recall a hadith today. It's not random, and it's definitely not just "old age" or a bad memory. There's a reason knowledge disappears. And it's tied to something most people never think about: a Zakah you owe on what you know - one that has nothing to do with money.

Skip it, and Abdullah Ibn al-Mubarak said one of three things happens to you. One of them is terrifying.

In this episode, Ustadh Muhammad Tim Humble breaks down:
- Why the Qur'an and knowledge you once had start slipping away
- The hidden "Zakah" scholars say you owe on your knowledge
- What actually happens when you don't pay it

description:
Some Names of Allah don't just describe Him. They expose the difference between Him and everything else that exists. This episode of Fiqh al-Asma al-Husna series centres on three connected Names: Al-Khaliq, Al-Bari' and Al-Musawwir.

These are Names that are brought together in the Quran in a single verse to describe how Allah brings everything into being.

Look at every skyscraper, every aircraft, every invention people are proud of. Impressive as it looks, none of it was "created"; it was only rearranged from what Allah had already made. So Allah throws down a challenge that no engineer, no scientist, and no civilisation has ever met:

Even if all of creation gathered together, they could not create a single fly.

So what does true creation actually mean? And why does this one distinction expose the falsehood behind every form of shirk?

The question is - if Allah alone brings things into existence from nothing, what does that mean for everything you fear, pursue, or place your trust in besides Him?

description:

Everything you see is marked by a beginning, a deficiency, an end, or weakness. But what of the One whose life was never preceded nor is His life touched by death, sleep, or any deficiency? The One who needs nothing… yet everything is sustained by Him.

These names don’t just describe Allah - they establish why He alone is worthy of worship, reliance, and Du'aa.

And hidden within them is a powerful reality… one that transforms how distress, hardship, and need are answered.

The question is - are you willing to truly understand them and find in your life a sudden burst of Tawakkul like never before?

description:

In this episode of Tafseer Juz 'Amma, Ustadh Muhammad Tim Humble walks through Surah 'Abasa - a Makki Surah that opens with a single overlooked moment and quietly unfolds into something that reaches every one of us.

What you'll learn in this episode:
- Who truly deserves our attention and who doesn't; and the danger of turning away from those who sincerely seek Allah's guidance
- The knowledge we carry and the responsibility that comes with it
- How Allah describes His Speech, the Quran - and what that should do to the way we treat it
- The story of a human being: created, sustained, guided at every turn - and still falling short of what Allah asked of him
- None of us has fulfilled what Allah commanded. So what right do any of us have to arrogance?

These lessons are not comfortable. But they are ones we cannot afford to miss.

description:
One day, your soul will be taken. No delay. No negotiation. It will simply be taken. The question is what it leaves behind. Allah reminds us in this Surah that you cannot hold on to both when they clash. Either the Dunya comes first, or the Akhirah does. There is no third option.

In this episode of Tafseer Juz Amma, Ustadh Muhammad Tim Humble walks through Tafseer of Surah An-Nazi'at, a Surah about the Resurrection, the reality of what comes after, and the choices that define which side you land on.

We reflect on the angels, the power of Allah over life and death, and the story of Musa and Fir'awn. A man who saw the signs clearly. Who was given every chance. And who still chose arrogance over submission. That's not just history. It's a mirror.

If Allah created the heavens without a single flaw, bringing you back to life is simple. The question was never whether it would happen. The question is what you did before it did.

Near the end of this Surah, a companion asked the Prophet ﷺ the same question people have always asked, when is the Hour? The Prophet ﷺ turned it back on him. One question. Three words. And it changes everything about how you're supposed to be living right now.

Watch to uncover what Ibn Rajab understood, and what every Muslim needs to reflect on today.

description:
They believed Allah created them. So why didn't they worship Him? It wasn't ignorance. They knew Allah gives life, controls the universe, and sends provision. But when it came to worshipping Him alone, they stopped. That same gap exists today.

And it starts with a Name you say in every prayer, every Dua, every day, but may never have truly understood:

Ar-Rabb.

Scholars say this Name is so vast, it carries the meaning of every other Name and Attribute of Allah within it. Once you see what it contains, your entire relationship with Him shifts.

There's a reason the Prophets used this Name when they called upon Allah. A reason it's the opening of the very first Surah. A reason it separates those who merely acknowledge Allah from those who truly worship Him.

Ustadh Muhammad Tim Humble explains what Ar-Rabb reveals about Allah's control, His nurturing, His perfect decree, and what changes when you finally grasp what you're saying when you call upon your Rabb.

A stark comparison sits beneath the words. A life measured in decades, set against a standing that stretches beyond imagination. Suddenly, the question isn’t what you’ve gained, but whether you’ve used your mind well enough to recognise what truly benefits you.

There’s a tension running through this lesson. Between time and value. Between effort and return. Between drifting through the Dunya and responding to a call that asks more of you than comfort ever will.

You’ll find yourself rethinking words you use lightly. Fortune. Gain. Success. Even intelligence. Are they really what you thought, or have they been shaped by a much shorter horizon?

description:
War was never the plan.
So how did the situation change so quickly?

The Muslims left Madinah intending to intercept a caravan. But once the caravan escaped, new information reached both sides, and the direction of events shifted.

In episode 76 of the Seerah, Ustadh Abdulrahman Hassan explains how matters developed as Quraysh continued advancing toward Badr. Their numbers, leadership, and intentions become clear, as does why some tribes chose to turn back while others pressed on.

The episode also follows the decisions made by the Prophet ﷺ as the reality of a battle became unavoidable. Consultation takes place, different opinions are voiced, and firm commitments are given by the companions, especially as responsibility settles on those who would bear the greatest cost.

You’ll learn how the Muslims prepared on the ground, how information was gathered, how positions were chosen near the wells of Badr, and how Allah supported them through the night with calm, rest, and stability.

The Prophet ﷺ spends the night in duʿa, while the army prepares for what lies ahead.

The battle has not begun yet.
But everything needed for it is now in place.

description:
The Name Allah appears more than two thousand times in the Qur’an. Let that sink in. It’s in almost every duʿa you make, every dhikr you repeat, every moment you turn back to your Lord. Yet most of us say it thousands of times in our lives without ever stopping to ask the simplest question.

Do I actually understand the One I’m calling upon?

We move from ayah to ayah, dhikr to dhikr, prayers, hopes, fears… all built on a Name we use constantly but rarely study. And that gap changes everything about our worship.

The Qur’an doesn’t teach you how to pray before it teaches you who you’re praying to. It begins with Names that carry the meanings of divinity, servitude, and the exclusive right to be worshipped.

Knowing these Names is not the end of your journey. It’s the moment it truly starts. Because once you know what they mean, another question hits even harder:

What do these Names ask from you?

In this episode, Ustadh Muhammad Tim Humble explores the Names Allah and Al-Ilah, and how understanding them reshapes worship, dependence, and the very way you see yourself as a servant of your Lord.

Everyone submits to Allah, willingly or unwillingly.
These Names reveal which path you’re really walking.

Watch this. Let it change how you worship.

Just enough is revealed to awaken the heart, not enough to soften the warning.

description:
The Dunya pushes you: “Earn more. Climb higher. Secure your future.”
Your heart quietly asks: "But when will you seek knowledge? What about the Akhirah?"

If you’ve ever watched your commitment to seeking knowledge fade while life pulls you in every direction… if you’ve ever stared at your week and wondered when your Iman slipped through the cracks… this poem was written for you.

Welcome to our new series on the Ta’iyyah of Abu Ishaq al-Ilbiri - a poem so striking that scholars across generations instructed their students to memorise it. Not because it's beautiful poetry, but because it slaps you awake.

Taught by Ustadh Muhammad Tim Humble, this series takes you into a masterpiece that speaks to the modern Muslim student - the one juggling university, work, household, and trying to hold onto their Deen in a world that doesn't make it easy.

This isn't just admonition. It's not a Sheikh telling you "you're doing it wrong."
It's a father confessing to his son: “These are the mistakes I made. These are the attachments that cost me. Don’t repeat them. Take the path I should have taken.”

The poem revolves around three unshakeable truths:
Zuhd - turning away from a Dunya designed to capture you
Seeking Knowledge - the treasure that fills the void when you stop chasing wealth and status
Purifying the Soul - Tawbah, return, and filling your heart with what Allah loves

In Episode 1, Ustadh Muhammad introduces the poem's background, its author's remarkable story, and begins unpacking the very first line:
"The days shatter your heart, piece by piece..."

Why does the poem begin with the heart, not the body, not time, but your heart? What happens when Iman wears out like old clothing? And what are the five actions that can renew a broken heart?

This episode sets the stage for a journey that will challenge every student of knowledge, every person who's felt the weight of "I'm not doing enough," and every Muslim who knows deep down: the dunya is winning, and I need to fight back.

description:
We live in a time where visibility feels like a requirement. We post every moment, turn every good deed into content, and treat being unseen like failure. But the Salaf lived the opposite. They hid their good deeds the way we hide our sins. They feared praise the way we fear embarrassment. They preferred the background while we desire the centre.

"Inspired by the Salaf" is a call to step back from the noise. To pull hearts out of the culture of visibility, where every deed becomes content and every moment feels like it needs an audience. This series takes you into the mindset of people who feared attention, who protected their sincerity like treasure, and who begged Allah to keep them unknown. These were the Muslims whose names never filled timelines, yet their deeds filled the heavens.

This series pulls us back to their path, where hearts didn’t crave likes, they craved Allah. Where people hid their deeds, checked their intentions, called themselves out before others did, and stepped away from the spotlight before it blinded them. In each episode, we rediscover what they feared, what they warned against, and how they guarded their Ikhlas long before the word “clout” existed.

In this opening episode, Shaykh Abubakar al Khalafi takes us straight to the heart of the issue: the desire to be seen. He tells us why the Salaf called fame a deadly disease, why they cried when their names appeared on fatwas, and how wanting recognition poisons sincerity inch by inch. It shows how desiring fame steals the sweetness of Iman, makes worship shallow, and leaves a person looking religious while feeling empty.

Watch this if you’ve ever checked who viewed your story. If you’ve posted a good deed and waited for reactions. If being unnoticed feels like being irrelevant. The Salaf have something to tell you - and it might be the reminder that saves your heart before it’s too late.

title: Saying This is Shirk?

description:
Imagine waking up one day and realising everything you believed was true… was a lie. The scariest part? You were convinced you were right the entire time. Ignorance isn’t harmless. It’s the disease that blinds a person while they believe they can see.

Across the world, Muslims have endless access to knowledge - reminders, verses, hadith, fatawa - all just a scroll away. Yet never has confusion been so widespread. Sins parade as “freedom.” Music is suddenly rebranded as “halal” by modern du‘āt despite clear proof to the contrary. Zina, alcohol, and misguidance are no longer shameful - they’re personal “choices,” “differences of opinion,” and “no big deal.”

The signs of the Hour flicker around us while people argue online. The guardians of knowledge diminish, and ignorance confidently rises to take their place - shaping beliefs, corrupting morals, and slowly dismantling the Ummah from within.

People feel confident discussing matters that once made the greatest Sahabah pause. Opinions replace evidence. Impulse replaces forbearance. Foolishness replaces understanding.

Ignorance isn’t just “not knowing.”
It is turning away from the truth when it comes.
It is rejecting what saves the soul.
It is the very reason past nations fell - even after witnessing miracles with their own eyes.
It is why some Muslims cannot recognise truth anymore - even when it stands clearly in front of them.
It is why sins feel easier than obedience.
It is why misguided voices sound convincing.
It is why the heart feels dark, heavy, and spiritually dead.

This lecture by Ustadh Abdulrahman Hassan dives deep into the Qur’an and Sunnah to expose:
• How ignorance destroys Iman
• Why it leads to shirk, sin, and moral collapse
• The spiritual blindness that blocks truth
• Why Allah turns away from those who turn away from knowledge
• The simple, powerful cures Allah has given us

So now, the real question comes to be - are you okay being ignorant?
Or will you revive your heart with the light Allah revealed?

description:
“Akhi, if you know a sister looking for marriage, can you recommend me?”
“Sheikh, I’m applying to an Islamic university. Could you write me a tazkiyah?”

We hear these requests all the time. And we think it’s just a favour, something small, like sharing sugar or lending a pen.

But what if your one reckless recommendation becomes the reason for a broken marriage, a failed partnership, or someone being trusted who never deserved it?

Today, Muslims hand out تزكيات like casual favours for friends, students, and colleagues without truly knowing who they’re vouching for, or realising the weight of that testimony before Allah.

Umar ibn al-Khattab رضي الله عنه once rejected a man’s testimony not because he lied, but because he didn’t know enough to speak the truth. That’s how serious a tazkiyah really is.

In this eye-opening reminder, Sheikh Dr. Asim Al-Qaryooti uncovers how easily a “good word” can turn into a burden on your scales and, more importantly, how to handle this trust the right way.

When should you speak? When should you stay silent? And how do you give a tazkiyah that’s honest, responsible, and pleasing to Allah?

Watch this before you give your next recommendation. It might not be as light as you think.

description:
Every day, Muslims chase something. A better job, a higher position, a name that people recognise. We tell ourselves it’s just “for financial stability” or “to give my family a good life”. But somewhere along the way, that chase stops being a means and becomes the purpose.

The Prophet ﷺ warned us about this chase in one terrifying image: two hungry wolves let loose upon a flock of sheep. Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, one of the great scholars of Islam, unpacked this hadith in his timeless work Dhamm al-Maal wal-Jaah — showing how the hunger for money and fame tears into the heart more viciously than wolves ever could.

But Ibn Rajab didn’t stop there.
He explained how these desires quietly grow, how they disguise themselves as “hard work” or “success,” and how they can make even acts of worship lose their sincerity. He exposed how wealth can blind, how status can corrupt, and how seeking leadership can ruin a person long before they realise it.

This 8-hour explanation isn’t just an old book lesson. It’s a mirror. A mirror for the 21st-century Muslim drowning in work, bills, and social media noise - chasing promotions, likes, and validation, all while the soul grows emptier.

So what happens when that hunger takes over?
When your career, your image, your “success” become the measure of your worth?
When even your acts of worship begin to seek attention instead of Allah’s pleasure?

And what does Islam truly say about living in the dunya without being consumed by it?

Find out through the words of Ibn Rajab, and rediscover what it means to be content, grounded, and truly rich in the sight of Allah.

description:
We spend years working on our careers, chasing promotions, saving for homes, building comfort for our families. From the outside, it looks like growth. But in the sight of Allah, what’s our real balance sheet?

At every Janazah, we feel it for a moment: watching someone lowered into the grave and thinking, “One day that’ll be me.” Yet within hours, we’re back to the grind. Back to chasing the same wealth and routines that won’t follow us past the soil.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that three things accompany every person to the grave: family, wealth, and deeds. But only one remains. The other two - the very things we obsess over - abandon us the moment we need them most.

So what are you really investing in? Your children and wealth, which stay behind? Or your deeds, which remain with you forever?

In this reminder, Ustadh Abdulrahman Hassan unpacks the Akhirah investment strategy every believer needs to hear:
- Why Abu Bakr رضي الله عنه became the greatest in just 30 years - not through more worship, but through the state of his heart.
- Why Hassan al-Basri warned that time with family and wealth is devastatingly short.
- What it means to own two houses - the one you obsess over now, and the one you’ll live in forever.
- And what really decides whether your grave becomes a garden of Jannah or a pit of Fire.

This isn’t about Dunya's net worth. It’s about the only net worth that matters. The one revealed when you’re lowered into the ground. What are you leaving behind?

description:
The expeditions had begun. Quraysh’s caravans - loaded with the wealth stripped from the Muslims in Makkah - became the new target. The first expeditions passed without major confrontation, but each one edged closer to the inevitable clash. Then came Nakhlah.

A sealed letter. A mission meant only to observe. Twelve men who suddenly found themselves standing at a crossroads: strike the caravan now and risk spilling blood in the sacred month, or let it pass and lose the chance forever. One arrow was loosed. A man fell. Captives were taken. The first spoils of war were in Muslim hands.

What followed shook everything. Accusations, anger, and uncertainty filled Madinah. Even the Muslims themselves were unsure of what had just happened - until revelation from Allah ﷻ descended, clarifying the truth and turning the tide.

In this episode, Ustadh Abdulrahman Hassan explores:
- The Prophet’s ﷺ earliest expeditions and why only the Muhajirun participated in them.
- The Nakhlah raid and its far-reaching consequences.
- A tender moment that gave ‘Ali رضي الله عنه the name Abu Turab, and a chilling prophecy about his fate.
- Lessons from deviation, and why the chains of scholarship protect the Ummah.

A single decision at Nakhlah pushed the Muslims closer to what Quraysh had long feared: open battle.

It’s not a set of abstract theories. These are practical principles shaping rulings on worship, contracts, business dealings, certainty and doubt, benefit and harm, and much more.

You’ll see how Islam doesn’t list rulings for every single case, but lays down timeless maxims that apply until the Day of Judgement. From conditions and reasons in worship, to why fasting is made up while prayers aren’t, to how scholars balance benefit against harm, this study opens the door to the science of fiqh.

If you want to move past surface-level answers and witness the beauty and consistency of Allah’s law, this poem will give you the tools to connect the dots.

description:
This poet once insulted the Prophet ﷺ — then stood before him, recited new verses… and walked away wearing the Prophet’s ﷺ cloak.

This is the true story of Banat Su’ad: a poem that turned an enemy into a forgiven companion. Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr was once known for mocking the Prophet ﷺ and attacking his family with his words. Fearing for his life, he came to Madinah, sat in front of the Prophet ﷺ, and asked, “If Kaʿb came to you now and accepted Islam, would you forgive him?”

When the Prophet ﷺ said yes, Kaʿb revealed himself and recited Banat Su’ad — a masterpiece of Arabic poetry, rich with imagery, fear, and hope. The Prophet ﷺ listened without interruption, moved by Kaʿb’s sincerity and eloquence. Then, in a moment that made history, he ﷺ removed his Burdah and placed it over Kaʿb’s shoulders — and the poem came to be known as Qaseedah al-Burdah.

In this video, Ustadh Abdulrahman Hassan unpacks the poem’s language, striking metaphors, and timeless lessons behind each verse. Witness how one poem turned mockery into mercy — and why Banat Su’ad is still recited and studied by seekers of knowledge to this day.

Grounded, clear, and relevant — this session provides practical guidance for Muslims navigating this topic today.

In Episode 1, Ustadh Abdulrahman Hassan breaks down the first hadith of the book—where the Prophet ﷺ says: “Do not prevent your women from the masājid, but their homes are better for them.”

- What exactly does this mean today?
- Is it really better for women to pray at home—even in Makkah and Madinah?
- Can a husband stop his wife from going to the masjid? And when is that allowed?
- What conditions did the scholars set for women going out—and are they still being met today?
- And what did Aisha رضي الله عنها say that still speaks volumes about modesty and change in society?

This isn’t just theory. It’s the lived fiqh of women—starting here.

Simultaneously, the Ustadh provides groundbreaking linguistic insights from the Hadith and explains how differences in understanding a single letter can lead to completely different meanings being extracted from it.

description:
In this 14th episode of ""The Disease And The Cure"", join us in a thought-provoking journey that examines the teachings of the Quran and the essence of true faith. Ustadh AbdulRahman Hassan discusses how blessings and hardships test believers and how one's response reveals their spiritual depth. This reminder encourages maintaining trust in Allah and embracing humility regardless of circumstances. The discussion highlights that the true value of a person is not measured by worldly success but by their faith and resilience.

The lecture also recounts the story of Qarun, whose unchecked wealth led to arrogance and ingratitude, illustrating how material gains can be deceptive. The importance of gratitude and recognizing Allah as the source of all blessings is underscored throughout the discussion. This serves as a cautionary tale, urging viewers to avoid the traps of pride and materialism that can lead one away from their spiritual path.

Finally, viewers are reminded of the temporary nature of this world compared to the eternal rewards of the hereafter. Ustadh then warns against being seduced by worldly praise and encourages a focus on seeking blessings through prayer and mindfulness. The video invites viewers to reflect on their priorities and strive to align their actions with the ultimate goal of attaining peace in the afterlife.

A few years after the construction of Masjid An-Nabawi, the Prophet ﷺ saw the growing needs of his expanding Ummah and initiated the first of many expansions of this sacred space—a Masjid he prophesied would be the last standing mosque on earth.

Ustadh also reflects on the virtues of the Ansar, beloved by the Prophet ﷺ for their sacrifice and support, reminding us of his ﷺ love and care for them. Filled with heartfelt reminders and moving prophecies, this episode inspires a deeper love for the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque and the early believers who first filled its walls.

Tune in to connect with the legacy of Masjid An-Nabawi and the timeless virtues of the Prophet’s ﷺ companions.

description:
Upon arriving in Madinah, why did the Prophet ﷺ prioritize building a mosque rather than a palace, home, or even a military base? What was the wisdom behind this choice?

In this episode of our Seerah series, Ustadh Abdulrahman Hassan explores the story of the construction of Masjid an-Nabawi.

Discover why the Prophet ﷺ insisted on purchasing the land for his Masjid instead of accepting it as a gift, and how he personally carried bricks alongside his companions—demonstrating humility and leadership in a way that touched every heart. 

Learn about a young companion who amazed everyone with his strength and dedication, and the touching story of a palm trunk that miraculously wept when a new pulpit replaced it as the Prophet’s ﷺ stand.

This episode also delves into the scholars’ debate on whether Madinah or Makkah holds greater virtue, highlighting the deep significance of the city the Prophet ﷺ made his home.

Join us for this powerful episode filled with history, wisdom, and timeless lessons on leadership, community, and worship. Don’t miss the opportunity to connect with the spirit of unity and devotion that built the foundation of the Muslim Ummah.

description:
Pharaoh had just watched Musa (as) perform a miracle. He couldn’t deny what the people saw, so he did something more subtle and effective: he labeled it as magic. One word, and the proof became a trick, the messenger became a suspect, and the argument was already tilted before anyone weighed the evidence.

In this Snapshot, Imam Tom Facchine unpacks how that same move still works today, as language frames the moral universe before a debate begins, and why Muslim leaders must learn to recognize when a word or a question is a trap. Drawing on the Qur’an’s close attention to names, labels, and accusations, he shows what it looks like to answer without accepting someone else’s frame.

This episode covers:
 — Why words like “extremism” and “moderation” aren’t neutral, and what they assume
 — Why some questions are built so that answering them means losing, and when a leader should reframe or refuse
 — Four questions to ask of any loaded word before you respond
 — Why Muslims need a moral vocabulary rooted in revelation

description:
Some hadith are hard to read and understand the first time around. 

One of them is the authentic narration in Bukhari and Muslim where the Prophet ﷺ says, “I was commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah.” Read alone, it can sound like an order of endless war against non-Muslims. The scholars who explained it read it a different way. In this hadith, “the people” refers to the pagan Arab tribes who broke treaty after treaty at the end of the Prophet’s ﷺ mission, not to all of humanity. The Qur’an sets peace as the default (“if they incline to peace, incline to it as well”). The Prophet ﷺ made treaties with non-Muslims and lived beside them in Medina. He also said to leave the Abyssinians and the Turks alone as long as they left the Muslims alone. In Islamic law, the justification for war is always protective. Its rules shield non-combatants, women, children, clergy, animals and even trees, and a promise of safety holds even when an eight-year-old gives it.

Hadith 9 of Imam al-Nawawi’s 40 draws our attention to a question: Why does the Prophet ﷺ tell us to avoid what he forbids completely, but to do what he commands “as much as you can”? Avoiding something takes no money and no strength, only will, so it is within everyone’s reach. Plenty of people do good deeds. Staying away from what Allah forbids is what sets a God-conscious person apart. The same hadith warns about questions asked to dodge an obligation, to trip someone up, or to look pious, like the man who asked Ibn ‘Umar about the blood of fleas. In this episode of Anchored: The 40 Hadith for Today’s Muslim, Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy explains what jihad really means in the Islamic tradition, how Islam’s ethics of war compare with other civilizations, and why closing the gap between what you know and what you do matters more than gathering another answer.

description:
"Does Islam permit a man to hit his wife?"

Islam condemns domestic violence, and a woman is never required to stay silent in the face of abuse. So how do we make sense of Quran 4:34, the verse Muslim women often wrestle with?

Yaqeen scholar Dr. Tesneem Alkiek and host Cadar Mohamud start with a key principle in the Islamic legal tradition: marriage never erased a woman’s independent legal identity. She owns property, enters contracts, and can take her husband to court when she is harmed. Dr. Alkiek explains how jurists defined that harm.

She then looks at what classical jurists actually said about physical discipline. That includes the strict limits they placed on it and how many of them advised men to avoid it entirely. The episode ends with the Prophet’s ﷺ example and what a woman should do when patience is the wrong response.

If you are struggling with despair, hopelessness, or thoughts of harming yourself, please contact Naseeha Mental Health for free, confidential, faith-sensitive support. Call or text 1-866-627-3342 or visit https://naseeha.org.

A narration says that before the Hour a man will pass a grave and say, “I wish I were in his place,” and that it will not be out of longing for Allah but out of exhaustion with life. 

The emptiness is the sign, not the hardship. What the same tradition carries is the correction: everyone already in a grave would trade everything they owned for one more day to seek Allah’s pleasure.

اللَّهُمَّ أَحْيِنِي مَا كَانَتْ الْحَيَاةُ خَيْرًا لِي وَتَوَفَّنِي إِذَا كَانَتْ الْوَفَاةُ خَيْرًا لِي
Allahumma ahyini ma kanat al-hayatu khayran li, wa tawaffani idha kanat al-wafatu khayran li.

description:
Manners are not the polish on top of a religion. 

In the framework Abdullah ibn Mubarak used, faith sits inside five concentric walls. Certainty at the centre, then sincerity, then the obligations, then the prophetic practices, and manners as the outermost wall of all. The order matters, because the outermost wall is the one that gets breached first. 

Lose your adab and the sunnah starts looking optional; lose the sunnah and the obligations start slipping; lose those and whatever worship is left is self-selected, which means it was never very sincere; and at the end of that sequence a person’s certainty is gone. Nobody experiences this as a collapse. It happens inward, in order, over years.

The practical edge of all this is uncomfortable, and Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy lands it hard at the end. Islam was built on five pillars, which makes those pillars infrastructure rather than decoration. Everything else is finishing work, and finishing work on a structure in shambles is not piety. It is decor.

“Anchored: 40 Hadith for Today’s Muslim” is a new series by Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy which draws insights from Imam an-Nawawi (rh)’s collection of 40 hadith and applies them to some of the most pressing questions Muslims face today.

Thirty Companions of the Prophet ﷺ each feared they might be a hypocrite. Not one of them dared say their faith matched the angels’. In this khutbah, Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy asks the question most people never ask themselves, and then shows why that righteous fear itself was the thing protecting them.

There is a kind of hope in Allah that has no actions behind it, and the Qur’an gives it a name: amaniyy. False hopes. Wishful thinking. It is the counterfeit of husn al-dhann billah, thinking well of Allah, and it is convincing precisely because it wears the same face. 

Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy walks through Surah Al-Hadid verse by verse to trace four steps of this delusion: you tempted yourself, you kept delaying, you began to doubt, and your false hopes deceived you.

If you have ever told yourself Allah is the Most Merciful and then quietly stopped obeying Him, this khutbah is a very urgent reminder.

These are some of the complicated questions that shape the decisions Muslims have to make every day, as students, professionals, parents, community members, and even in their personal worship. 

And answering them starts with reflecting on the foundation of everything we do in life: intention (niyyah). 

After introducing us to the great scholar Imam an-Nawawi (rh), Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy explains what every Muslim must know about intention. 

“Anchored: 40 Hadith for Today’s Muslim” is a new series by Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy which draws insights from Imam an-Nawawi (rh)’s collection of 40 hadith and applies them to some of the most pressing questions Muslims face today. 

Tune in every Saturday at 9 AM CST/3 PM GMT for a new episode of Anchored!

Episode 1 covers the first hadith: The Prophet ﷺ said, “Actions are according to intentions, and everyone will get what they intended. Whoever migrates with an intention for Allah and His messenger, the migration will be for the sake of Allah and his Messenger. And whoever migrates for worldly gain or to marry a woman, then his migration will be for the sake of whatever he migrated for.” [Sahih al-Bukhari 54]

description:
Six months after 9/11, 25% of Americans said Islam encourages violence more than other religions. 25 years later, that number is 51%.

The hostility did not fade with time. It grew. And it grew in a country where Muslims buried their own dead from that day, where Muslim first responders ran toward the towers, and where a generation has now spent its entire life answering for a crime committed by 19 strangers.

On the 25th anniversary of September 11th, Sh. Omar Suleiman takes the question America asked in 2001 and turns it in the other direction. Why do they hate us? Who taught you to hate?

This khutbah sits with collective blame and what the Qur'an says about it. Allah tells us that no soul carries the burden of another (Surah al-An'am, 6:164). He commands justice even toward people who despise us: “Do not let the hatred of a people lead you away from justice. Be just. That is closer to taqwa.” (Surah al-Ma'idah, 5:8).

For Muslims who have never known an America before the Patriot Act, the watchlist, and the secondary screening line at the airport, this is a khutbah about where the hate actually came from, who has profited from keeping it alive, and why the enemy you were handed may not be your enemy at all.

Sources: https://www.pewresearch.org/newsletter/religion-weekly/25-years-after-9-11-a-portrait-of-muslim-americans/

description:
Shaytan never told Adam and Hawwa (as) to disobey Allah. He told them the forbidden tree was something else: shajarat al-khuld, the tree of eternal life. A good tree.

The command never changed. Only the name did. The Prophet ﷺ warned that this technique would come back at the end of time as one of the signs of the Hour, and it's stranger than it first sounds. It isn't about a generation that stops believing in halal and haram. It's about a generation that keeps both categories perfectly intact and quietly moves things between them. People from this ummah will drink khamr, he ﷺ said, and call it by another name.

Imam al-Ghazali (rh) mapped the same move through the diseases of the heart centuries before anyone said the word “rebrand”. Greed is renamed as ambition. Arrogance has been renamed to confidence. Cutting off your family answers to protecting your peace.

Dajjal is the end of this road, not the beginning of it. He'll rebrand Jannah as the Fire and kufr as imaan. A world that's spent generations learning to accept renamed evil is already rehearsed for him.

Name every major sin you can think of, then ask which ones already answer to something softer. That's the exercise Dr. Omar Suleiman puts to the room, and it's worth doing before you press play.

description:
You may still be alive tomorrow, but this version of your life won’t be.

Your body will change. Your circumstances will change. Your children will grow older. Your parents may not always be here. The person waiting for your apology may eventually stop waiting.

So what happens to all the good we keep telling ourselves we’ll do later?

The call we keep meaning to make. The apology we keep putting off. The time we assume we’ll have with our parents and children. The charity we tell ourselves we’ll give tomorrow.
The Qur’an preserves the plea of someone who ran out of time:

“My Lord, if only You would delay me for a little while, I would give in charity and be among the righteous.” — (Surah Al-Munafiqun, Verse 10)

But the delay never comes.

This isn’t simply a warning about dying suddenly. It’s a reminder that some of the good we postpone depends on having the right person, the right moment, or the right opportunity still in front of us.

In this khutbah, Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on time, aging parents, growing children, unfinished apologies, and the opportunities for goodness we assume will still be there tomorrow.
What have you been putting off because you assume you’ll have more time?

description:
There was an eclipse on one of the most painful days of the Prophet ﷺ's life. He reminded the ummah about the eclipse prayer.

How to pray Salat al-Kusuf (the eclipse prayer):

It's 2 rak’ahs, prayed in congregation if possible. No adhan or iqamah.

In each rak’ah: Recite Surah al-Fatihah + a long surah, then a long ruku, then rise and recite al-Fatihah + another surah again, then bow a second time, then go into sujood as normal. So each rak’ah has 2 standings, 2 bowings, and 2 prostrations.

After the prayer, it's sunnah to give a khutbah reminding people of Allah's power, as the Prophet ﷺ did. 

Beyond the prayer, it's sunnah to make du’a and dhikr until the eclipse ends, give charity, and seek Allah’s forgiveness.

description:

But think about the people you love most. Sometimes the gift isn’t what they give you. It’s the fact that you’re with them.

Allah says you ask and He is close. Then He says you ask and He answers. Nearness comes before response. Love comes before provision.

description:
In July 1995, more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were executed after Srebrenica, a United Nations-declared "safe zone," fell to Bosnian Serb forces. Recognized as genocide by international courts, it remains the worst atrocity on European soil since 1945. 

In this documentary, Dr. Omar Suleiman travels from Sarajevo to Srebrenica, where the scars of genocide remain etched into the landscape and the lives of those who survived it. Through the stories of those left behind, we remember what happened, examine what justice looks like decades later, and ask what Bosnia's past can teach us as many witness similar horrors unfolding in Gaza today.

Produced by Osama Rkieh. A special note of gratitude to the Srebrenica Memorial Center and to Islamic Relief Canada for facilitating the visits to the families.

اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الثَّبَاتَ فِي الأَمْرِ وَالْعَزِيمَةِ عَلَى الرُّشْدِ وَأَسْأَلُكَ شُكْرَ نِعْمَتِكَ وَحُسْنَ عِبَادَتِكَ وَأَسْأَلُكَ قَلْبًا سَلِيمًا وَلِسَانًا صَادِقًا وَأَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ خَيْرِ مَا تَعْلَمُ وَأَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا تَعْلَمُ وَأَسْتَغْفِرُكَ لِمَا تَعْلَمُ

Allahumma inni as’aluka ath-thabbata fi’l-amr wa’l-ʿazimata ʿala’r-rushdi wa as’aluka shukra niʿmatik wa husna ʿibadatik wa as’aluka qalban saliman wa lisanan sadiqan wa as’aluka min khayri ma taʿlamu wa aʿudhu bika min sharri ma ta'lamu wa astaghfiruka lima taʿlam.

O Allah, I ask You for steadfastness in all my affairs and determination in following the right path, I ask You to make me thankful for Your blessings and to make me worship You properly. description:
How can you protect yourself from the Dajjal, and the era of dajalah (deception) that comes before him? 

The Prophet ﷺ gave us guidance for our protection from these trials, including multiple du’as and 20 verses from Surah al-Kahf — and he taught us to make sure that we don’t become agents of deception today.  

Here is a du’a he ﷺ taught us for when we leave home every day: 

اللّهُـمَّ إِنِّـي أَعـوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَضِـلَّ أَوْ أُضَـل أَوْ أَزِلَّ أَوْ أُزَل أَوْ أَظْلِـمَ أَوْ أَُظْلَـم أَوْ أَجْهَلَ أَوْ يُـجْهَلَ عَلَـيّ

Allahumma 'inni 'aʿudhu bika 'an 'adilla, 'aw 'udalla, 'aw 'azilla, 'aw 'uzalla, 'aw 'adhlima, 'aw 'udhlama, 'aw 'ajhala 'aw yujhala ʿalayya.

O Allah, I seek refuge in You lest I misguide others, or I am misguided by others, lest I cause others to err or I am caused to err, lest I abuse others or be abused, and lest I behave foolishly or meet with the foolishness of others.

[Abu Dawud, hadith no. 5075]

And a du’a to read at the end of your salah:

اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ عَذَابِ جَهَنَّمَ وَمِنْ عَذَابِ الْقَبْرِ وَمِنْ فِتْنَةِ الْمَحْيَا وَالْمَمَاتِ وَمِنْ شَرِّ فِتْنَةِ الْمَسِيحِ الدَّجَّالِ

Allahumma inni aʿudhu bika min ‘adhabi jahannama, wa-min ʿadhabi-l-qabri, wa-min fitnati-l-mahya wa-l-mamati, wa-min sharri fitnati-l-masihi-d-dajjal.

O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of Hell, from the punishment of the grave, from the trials of life and death, and from the evil trial of the False Messiah.

[Sahih Muslim, hadith no. 588]

Arab Christians have used the word Allah to refer to God for over a thousand years. It's in their Bibles. It's in their churches. It always has been.
Using it as a punchline on the holiest morning of the Christian calendar says less about Islam than it does about how little we know about it.

description:
For the last 30 days, we’ve been on a journey, learning the Names of Allah. Each Name is more than a word. It’s a way of being, a lesson in how to live. We wanted to inspire you, our audience, not just to memorize them, but to connect with them deeply, to see how they show up in the world around us.

This micro-drama is based on the true story of a family from Gaza. As we’ve been witnessing our brothers and sisters there and beyond over the last few years, we see those Names in action. Patience, trust, resilience, tawakkul in its purest form. We see As-Sabur in their patience and Al-Wakeel in the way they place their trust in Allah. They don’t leave, they endure, and in their steadfastness we find lessons that speak far beyond words.

We also hold in our hearts all those around the world who face hardship and oppression. Their courage and perseverance reminds us that the Names of Allah are not just lessons to learn, but realities being lived, wherever hearts remain steadfast.

Alhamdulillah for every one of you who has joined us on this journey, reflected with us, and felt alongside us. Thank you for witnessing, for opening your hearts, and for carrying these lessons forward. May we see the Names of Allah in our own actions, in patience under pressure, in trust through difficulty, and in steadfastness when the world tests us.

description:
If you're standing at the end of this month wondering how to carry what you found here into everything that comes next — follow along with this du'a:

Ya Allah,
When I forget even myself, let Your name always remain in my heart and on my tongue. And let my heart always find its way back to You. When I call You by this Name, I am calling every mercy, every promise, every door that leads home. You are what no one else is. And for me, what no one else can be.

Ya Hayy,
The Ever-Living who never fades. Put life into my worship when it starts to fade, and life into my purpose when I start to feel lost again. Let my faith in You stay alive when the world floods me with dying promises, and the devil deceives with his deception.

Ya Qayyum,
The Sustainer of all that exists. Hold me together when I fall apart. Sustain my heart with Your remembrance, and my deeds with sincerity. Do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye. Steady me when I swerve, with Your guidance. Receive me when I return, with Your grace.

Ya Allah,
When I rise from one of Your seasons of incredible mercy, let me remember that You were always Merciful from the beginning. And You will always be in the end, so long as I return to You.
Ya Allah, return me to You.
Ya Allah, return me to You.
Ya Allah, return me to You.
In the presence of Your beloved ﷺ and all those who knew You the way I want to. In the beginning and the end and always, to You all praise is due. Ameen.

In this series finale, Dr. Omar Suleiman unpacks the Greatest Name of Allah and its most powerful pairing. Allah, Al-Hayy, Al-Qayyum. The Ever-Living. The Ever-Sustaining. The Name that gathers every other Name. The one that, when you say it with your heart, every door opens.

Al-Hayy speaks to His perfect existence. His knowledge never pauses. His hearing never dulls. His sight never weakens. When you call on Him in the middle of the night, He is not tired. When a billion people call on Him at once, He is not overwhelmed.

Al-Qayyum speaks to His perfect sustaining of everything He created. Every breath you take, every beat of your heart, every cell in your body functions only because He holds it in place. He does not create and leave. He creates and keeps.

Say farewell to Ramadan. But step forward into a lifetime of knowing the One who was always there, always listening, and always yours.

Ya Awwal,
You were there before beginnings were written. Before my first breath, You already knew my name. Remind me that nothing starts without You, and that every good I begin is only by Your permission. Let my first step in anything always be towards You.

Ya Aakhir,
You remain when all else fades. When every name is forgotten, Yours endures. Let my last breath be in Your remembrance, and my last sight be upon Your mercy.

Ya Dhaahir,
You are evident in every beauty, in the rise of the sun and the appearance of the moon. Let me see Your majesty in all that surrounds me, until everything I witness becomes a door back to You.

Ya Baatin,
You are nearer than my thoughts, closer than my pulse. You know the things I can't say, and forgive the things I can't hide. Preserve me in the unseen as You do in the open, and let my nearness to You outlast my time on this earth. Ameen.

Ramadan felt like a blink. One day your whole life will too.

In this episode, Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on four Names of Allah that reframe everything you feel at the end of Ramadan. The guilt of wasted nights. The panic of time slipping. The fear that none of it was enough. Al-Awwal, Al-Aakhir, Az-Zaahir, Al-Baatin. The First and the Last. The Manifest and the Hidden. Four names in a single breath that frame your entire existence from beginning to end.

He was there before your first breath and He will be there when you take your last. You did not stumble into existence by accident. You were thought of, designed, and intended. And every moment you have lived has been under His eternal gaze. When you feel like you are running out of time, remember that the One who started everything started you too.

He is evident in every sunrise, every moment of protection, every relief after a despair you thought would never end. And He is nearer than your thoughts, closer than your pulse. He knows the fear before you name it and the hope you are too ashamed to say out loud. You are never alone. Not in your highest moment. Not in your lowest.

And when time feels like it is running out, the Prophet (PBUH) said that if the final hour arrives and you are still holding a seed, plant it. You will not see it grow. You will not taste its fruit. But nothing you do for Allah is ever wasted.

Even if the world is ending, plant the seed.

If your heart feels like it's in pieces, if distance and time have separated what you love, or if you're wondering what will remain of you when you're gone, follow along with this du'a:

Ya Hayiyy,
You are too shy to turn away these hands. How many times have I asked with nothing worthy in return, and yet still You answered in a way that left me in awe. When I stand before You ashamed, forgive me for my mountains of fault through a little of Your mercy, and give me more than I dare to ask because of Your generosity.

Ya Jaami',
Gather the pieces of my heart that the world has broken. Or perhaps I myself have broken. Unite what distance and time have separated. Bring together my past and my purpose, my loved ones and the reward You've promised, until we meet again under the shade of Your throne, complete.

Ya Waarith,
As everything returns to You, what fades for me remains preserved with You. Keep my deeds when I am gone and let them grow. And my legacy when I'm forgotten, so long as not by You. Inherit my soul with Your pleasure, and leave behind only what You'll love to return to me. Ameen.

description:
The end of Ramadan is a time to redouble your efforts. Support Yaqeen in these final 10 nights: http://yqn.io/c65i

What if one sentence could erase your entire record?

On Laylatul Qadr, our mother Aisha (RA) did not ask for a list. She asked one question. The Prophet (PBUH) did not give her a ladder to climb or a prayer to memorize. He gave her one name of Allah, one attribute, and one ask: O Allah, You are Al-'Afuww, the Pardoner. You love to pardon. So pardon me.

In this episode, Dr. Omar Suleiman draws a clear line between Al-Maghfirah, forgiveness, and Al-'Afuww, pardon. Forgiveness covers a sin and protects you from its consequence. Pardon removes the trace entirely, as if the sin never existed. The scholars describe it as a wind sweeping the desert floor so that not even a footprint remains. That is the level of mercy this supplication is reaching for, and it is available to anyone who asks with a sincere heart on Laylatul Qadr.

The story of Abu Bakr (RA) and his relative Mustah brings this out of theology and into real life. Mustah was someone Abu Bakr financially supported, and he was among those who slandered the Prophet's wife, Aisha (RA). When Abu Bakr found out, he cut off the support. Allah then revealed a verse asking whether Abu Bakr would not love for Allah to pardon him. Abu Bakr did not just forgive Mustah. He restored everything he had been giving him, as if nothing had ever happened. That is what Al-'Afuww looks like when it lives inside a person.

Dr. Omar also walks through the Sunnah practice of seeking pardon three times every single day, through the morning and evening remembrances and the final two verses of Surah Al-Baqarah before sleep. These are not just rituals. They are a daily conversation with the one Name of Allah that can wipe a record clean and open every door that sin has closed.

This episode begins with a personal dedication from one brother to another, asking him to care for someone they both love. It is a reminder that on the nights when we carry the heaviest things to Allah, we do not come alone.

description:

Have you ever looked at someone else’s life and wondered why blessings seem to reach them so easily while you struggle to receive? Many people quietly carry questions like whether Allah truly loves them, why hardship keeps appearing in their lives, or why it sometimes feels like their du‘as are unanswered.

Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on three of the most hope-giving Names of Allah: Al-Jawaad, Al-Mannaan, and Al-Wahhaab. Through these Names we begin to understand how Allah’s generosity works, how divine blessings unfold in our lives, and why what feels like delay or hardship is not a sign of rejection.

The Qur’an reminds us that Allah gives in ways that go far beyond human logic. Sometimes His generosity appears as visible blessings. Other times it appears as guidance, forgiveness, or protection from things we never saw coming. These Names reveal a Lord who gives before we ask, reshapes lives with immense favors, and grants gifts purely out of love and mercy.

For anyone wrestling with feelings of unworthiness, sadness, or spiritual heaviness, these Names offer a powerful reminder that Allah’s generosity continues even when our circumstances feel uncertain. Understanding blessings in Islam through the Names of Allah transforms how we see hardship, gratitude, and hope.

By reflecting on Al-Jawaad (The Most Generous), Al-Mannaan (The Bestower of Favors), and Al-Wahhaab (The Giver of Gifts), we are reminded that Allah’s mercy reaches us before our hands are raised, His favors reshape our stories, and His gifts are granted far beyond what we could ever deserve.

Ya ‘Adheem,
my Lord of Might without measure. Make my reverence for You heavier than any fear of creation. Let my heart bow before You long before my body does. and let my most unstable positions be still by my trust in You.

description:
Most people treat prayer like another task squeezed into an already crowded day. Something to get through quickly before returning to everything else demanding attention.

But salah was never meant to compete with your life. It was meant to interrupt it.

Throughout the day, responsibilities pile up, conversations pull your focus, and worries slowly fill the mind. Without noticing it, the heart begins to revolve entirely around the world.

Salah breaks that cycle.

Five times a day, everything pauses. The schedule stops, the noise fades, and you step away from people, obligations, and distractions to stand before the One who gave you the day itself.

Those few minutes are not a burden on your time. They are a mercy placed within it.

Because a heart left in the dunya all day begins to suffocate. And salah is the moment Allah gives you to breathe again.

Watch Episode 25 of “The Name I Need” to learn more: https://yqn.io/q64f

Salah is not meant to interrupt life. It's meant to reorient it.

In this episode, Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on the deeper meaning of prayer through the Names of Allah revealed in every movement of salah. From the opening declaration of “Allahu Akbar,” reflecting the greatness of Al-Kabeer, to bowing in ruku before Al-’Adheem, to finding closeness in sujood with Al-A’laa, and finally greeting Al-Majeed in the closing of the prayer, salah becomes a journey through the greatness, majesty, and glory of Allah.

Through powerful reflections on the universality of prayer, the rhythm of the five daily prayers, and the way salah pulls the believer out of distraction and back into remembrance, this episode explores why prayer is one of the greatest sources of grounding and spiritual clarity in Islam.

For anyone wondering why Muslims pray five times a day, how to find focus in salah, or how prayer brings peace in the middle of a busy world, this reflection reveals how the Names of Allah transform every posture of prayer into a moment of presence with Him.

description:
Most people imagine patience as one moment of restraint. A single decision to stay calm when something difficult happens.

But sabr isn’t just one reaction. It quietly appears across different parts of a believer’s life.

Sometimes patience shows up when you walk away from a temptation you could easily have taken. Sometimes it appears in hardship, when pain doesn’t turn you bitter or reckless. Other times it’s the quiet consistency of continuing a good deed long after the motivation fades.

Patience is also what allows a person to rebuild after failure instead of staying down. It’s the ability to start again after a mistake, a loss, or a disappointment.

And perhaps the hardest form of patience is the patience we show people. The restraint we practice when others frustrate us, misunderstand us, or test our limits.

Remembering how patient Allah has been with us often makes that last one easier.

Watch Episode 24 of our Ramadan Series now: https://yqn.io/jo7m
title: Where Patience Shows Up in Your Life

description:
The end of Ramadan is a time to redouble your efforts. Support Yaqeen in these final 10 nights: http://yqn.io/c65i

What do you do when the people around you keep testing your limits?

Patience in Islam isn’t weakness. The Prophet ﷺ said that no one has ever been given a gift more vast than patience. But patience isn’t simply waiting. It shows itself in how we control anger, endure hardship, and deal with difficult people without losing our integrity.

In this episode, Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on the Divine Names As-Saboor (The Most Patient), Al-Haleem (The Forbearing), Al-‘Aliyy (The Most High), and Al-Muta’aaly (The Supremely Exalted). Through these Names, we’re reminded that Allah’s patience with us should shape how we respond when others test us.

Patience appears in different moments of a believer’s life. Sometimes it’s resisting a temptation even when it’s within reach. Sometimes it’s enduring hardship without losing trust in Allah. And sometimes it’s remaining calm when someone’s behavior pushes you toward anger.

If you’ve ever struggled with anger or wondered how to deal with difficult people without losing yourself in the process, this reflection speaks directly to that experience. Islam doesn’t ask us to suppress emotion or ignore injustice. It teaches us how to rise above it without losing our character.

Allah sees every moment of restraint that no one else notices. Every time you hold back your anger, remain steady in hardship, or choose dignity over retaliation, it matters. The Qur’an promises that those who are patient will be rewarded without measure.

When you feel provoked, overwhelmed, or small in the face of difficult people, remember who is above it all. Allah sees what you can’t see, knows what you don’t know, and rewards patience in ways far greater than we can imagine.

Watch this reflection to rediscover the strength of patience and how faith teaches us to rise above anger, hardship, and the people who test us the most.

description:
We live in a time where healing feels almost entirely mechanical. You feel pain, you see a doctor, you receive treatment, and if things improve the credit usually goes to the medicine or the procedure.

Islam doesn’t reject any of those means. In fact, it encourages us to seek them. But it quietly corrects the way the heart understands them. A doctor can diagnose, prescribe, and treat, but the ability for a body to recover was never in their hands to begin with.

Every recovery, every closing wound, every fever that breaks, and every illness that lifts happens only because Allah allows the body to heal.

That’s why the Prophet ﷺ taught us to ask Allah as Ash-Shaafy, the One who heals completely. Not the One who merely reduces pain for a moment, but the One who can restore entirely and remove harm in ways no medicine can guarantee.

So the believer takes the means seriously, but the heart never attaches itself to the means. The prescription may be in the doctor’s hand, but healing itself remains with Allah.

Watch Episode 23 of ''The Name I Need'' with Dr. Omar Suleiman: yqn.io/ct5x
